newsitem.title: IRAQ: Iraq and Russia sign $70 bln oil deal over 23 years.
newsitem.headline: Iraq and Russia sign $70 bln oil deal over 23 years.

text.p: Iraq and Russia signed on Friday a contract to develop seven to eight billion barrels of reserves in southern Iraq's Qurana oilfield, Iraqi and Russian officials said.

"Now we have signed a contract to develop an oilfield with a production capacity of 600,000 barrels per day," Iraq's oil minister Amir Mohammed Rasheed said during the signing of the deal with visiting Russian Fuel and Enregy Minister Pyotr Rodionov.
Rodionov said the contract would be implemented regardless of the United Nations sanctions imposed on Iraq for its 1990 invasion of Kuwait.
The curbs place a blanket ban on Iraqi exports and investments in the country. The U.N. has allowed Iraq to pump $2 billion worth of oil over six months on humanitarian grounds.
"Execution of the contract will start regardless of the lifting of the economic sanctions," the Russian minister said.
Rasheed said the west of Qurana oilfield, 500 km (300 miles) south of Baghdad, had estimated reserves of seven to eight billion barrels and the deal would be implemented over 23 years.

"The reserve of Qurana oilfield second stage, which we have signed as a contract is approximately seven to eight billion barrels of oil. The production a day will be 600,000 barrels and the total revenue for Iraq over 23 years would be approximately 70 billion dollars," Rasheed said.
He said work to develop the oilfield would start "soon after the approval of both (Iraqi and Russian) goverments and parliaments."
Rodionov put cost of constructing the project at $3.5 billion without saying how that amount would be paid and by whom.
The Russian minister said on Thursday the deal would needs a few weeks before it could be signed.
"We had the conclusion that we need several weeks to resolve obstacles...but the real time was far less than that," he said after signing the pact.

Rasheed described the contract as "strategic and huge", said it was "big historic event" to "translate into deed President Saddam Hussein's directive that the first deal to develop an oilfield should be with Russia."
He said that Iraq hoped to sign similar contracts with other friendly countries, without naming them. France and China are also eager to strike deals with Baghdad to develop oilfields.
Moscow supports lifting all curbs on Iraqi oil exports and hopes Baghdad would be able to repay debts worth billions of dollars.
"Signing of this contract has raised the level of relations between the two countries," Rodionov said.
